bob-baker-vidalia-1915-08.A2:
THREE HELD IN MURDER CASE.
Feeling Runs High Against Negroes at Vidalia, Miss.
NATCHEZ, Miss., August 14—Bob Baker, his wife and King Lyon, all negroes, are in jail at Vidalia, near here, today on charges connected with the murder Thursday of Walter Simmerman, lumber mill owner of Concordia parish, La. Simmerman's body was found in the woods near his mill yesterday.

According to the coroner Baker confessed he killed Simmerman to rob him and implicated his wife and Lyon in the crime. All three were employed by Simmerman.

A special guard has been placed at the Vidalia jail, as the killing is reported to have aroused high feeling against the negroes.

Mill Man's Death a Mystery.
Natchez.—Walter Simmerman, wellknown
sawmill man, was mysteriously
murdered near his home, four miles
from Fish Pond and 20 miles from
Natchez, some time during the day of
Aug.. 12. The body was not found
until late in the night. Simmerman
had been shot with a shotgun, apparently
his own weapon. His neck had
been broken and the top of his head
blown off. He wa# found in a woods
lot some distance from his home. The
baying of his dogs drew the searchers
to the spot where his body lay. Simmerman
was a recluse. He came from
Danville, 111., about six years ago,
and had conducted a sawmill business
near Fish Pond ever since. So far as
known, Simmerman had no enemies,
and the motive for the murder if
shrouded in mystery.
Boy Drowns in Lake.
Summit.—The only son, a*10-year-old
boy, of Mr. and Mrs. Carey Dunn of
this place, was drowned in the lake
at the Godbold mineral well Aug. 12.
The body was under the water in the
middle and deepest part of the lake
for over an hour before it could be
found. Dr. L. F. Scott, a dentist of
this place, found the' little fellow by
letting himself down feet foremost.

hours threatened the entire plant.
Employes said the explosion of a
lamp caused the blaze. The damage
was estimated at more than $30,000

MOB'S TRICK FAILS.
Natchez, Miss., Aug. 24.—With his prisoners in a skiff, Sheriff Campbell of Concordia parish rowed across the Mississippi river last night and foiled a mob attempting to force the jail of Concordia parish.

The prisoners are Bob Baker, his wife and Jim Lyons, all negroes, who, the confessions state, murdered Walter Simmerman, wealthy sawmill owner, recently for $20.

The mob before attacking the jail, tried to trick the sheriff and get him out of the way by sending a message that a murder had been committed in a certain remote part of the parish.

The sheriff suspected something wrong, and refused to go. Instead he hurried his prisoners from the jail and to the skiff.

Arriving on the Mississippi side of the river he took the negroes to the Adams county pail and Monday morning departed with them to parts unknown.
bob-baker-vidalia-1915-08.A7:
MISSISSIPPI STATE BRIEFS
Meridian. — Benjamin F. Adcock, who was shot on the night of Aug. 22 by C. R. Fewox, died Aug. 28 at a hos pital. Fewox claims the unwritten law as his defense. The grand jury is investigating the case while Fewox is in jail.

Meridian.—A charge of attempted assault is placed against O. E. Halbert, and B. A. Schneider of Laurel on the docket of Justice Moody Price of this city. The two men had been placed under bond in Laurel pending action of the grand jury here. Both are prominent in Laurel. The accused men deny the charges, and claim that it is a case of attempted blackmail.

Meridian.—Alleging that her stepfather, M. J. Quigley, a machinist, knocked her down and that he had mistreated his wife, her mother, Mrs. A. J. Hatch on Aug. 22 fired a bullet from a 38-calibre pistol into the stomach of Quigley, who is at a local hospital and not expected to live. Owing to the fact that Mrs. Hatch has two small children, she was placed under arrest, but allowed to stay at home pending the result of her stepfather's wounds.

Columbus.—T. W. Townsend of this city has invented and perfected a machine which, in all probability, is the most effective mechanical device yet evolved with which to cope the boll weevil. Actual tests have demonstrated the merits of the machine. The machine is so constructed that the cotton is not damaged in the least and its use in several fields in cotton of varying heights show that the weevils are effectively collected. The machine also collects the punctured squares. It is light in weight and can be moved rapidly over the field.

Meridian.—Mrs. Oscar McDonald, a young matron of this city, was discovered Aug. 23 gagged and tied to a post in the basement of her mother's home at this place. Mrs. McDonald had just a few moments previously gone down into the basement to look up an old paper. She sat down on the steps, when a young white man suddenly threw a handkerchief across her mouth, seized her arms, pinioned them behind her, tied her wrists and then tied her hands to a post. He had just seized one of her fingers and was trying to pull off a fine diamond ring, when her mother, Mrs. S. C. Gordon, heard a muffled cry, and started down in the basement. As she did so the man ran out of the basement door and disappeared. Mrs. Gordon released her daughter, who was badly frightened, and whose wrists were severely cut by the cord which bound them. The police were unable to locate a trace of the intruder.

Natchez.—An attempt to lynch Bob Baker and King Lyons, negroes, held at Vidalia and charged with the murder of Walter Zimmerman near Fish Pond on Aug. 12, was frustrated by Sheriff Eugene Campbell and the prisoners brought to Natchez in a skiff. They were kept in jail her over night and then hurried to another place, supposedly Tallulah. It is said that an attempt was made to induce the sheriff to leave Vidalia by those who wished to lynch the negroes. A telephone message to him, it is said, stated that a murder had been committed some distance from Vidalia and that he was wanted at once. The suspicions of the officer had been aroused, however, and he did not go. The murder of Zimmerman was cold blooded and brutal. Baker, who confessed to the murder and implicated Lyons, was employed by Zimmerman, and shot him down to rob him. When arrested $20 was found in the sweat band of the negroe's hat. Using this as evidence, the officers forced him to tell the details.

The Bludwine Bottling Company of Hattiesburg suffered the loss of its plant on the night of Aug. 19, when the building and its contents burned. The fire which was discovered in the roof of the building, completely gutted the structure. John McDevitt, manager in charge, estimates the loss at $2,500, with $400 insurance on stock and fixtures.

The most extensive and energetic campaign that has ever been waged in Meridian in behalf of a civic organization was brought to a close on Aug. 20 at the Board of Trade when it was reported that more than 380 members had been signed for three years in the reorganization of the Board of Trade. This makes the organization stronger than it has ever been.

Walter Moffett was seriously injured in a runaway accident two miles each of Blue Mountain Aug. 19, when his buggy horse became frightened at an automobile driven by Cliff Dickson. Mr. Moffett had gotten out of the buggy to hold the horse and the frightened animal dragged him several hundred feet, hurled him against a stump and ran over him, dragging the buggy across his chest. He was brought to the home of his brother, Prof. M. E. Moffett, of Blue Mountain his ribs were fractured.

A cyclone struck McAdams, a small station seven miles west of Kosciusko, on the afternoon of Aug. 20, destroying the railroad station house, a seed house, the residence of Mrs. Francis Gowan and the mill shed of Gowan Bros., and doing other damage. A negro cabin on the Gowan farm, where five negroes were housed, was blown to pieces and the negroes left sitting in the rain, unhurt. No one was hurt in Mr. Gowan's house except his little daughter, who sustained a bruised shoulder

A case of mistaken identity that threatened a lynching developed at Meridian Aug. 20, when James Whitehead and Norman Elliott, two negroes, were arrested and placed in the county jail on a charge of attempting to assault Mrs. Curtis Robertson, wife of a well known citizen, as she was returning in a buggy with her baby from a visit to Causeyville on Aug. 15. Two other negroes, Willie Kirksey and Ben Boney, were arrested after being identified by Mrs. Robertson, and were placed in the county jail.

fat-ward-greer-1915-08.A1:
IN THE PALMETTO STATE
SOME OCCURRENCES OF VARIOUS KINDS IN SOUTH CAROLINA.
State News Boiled Down for Quick Reading.—Paragraphs About Men and Happenings.
A bale of new cotton was sold at Allendale on Saturday.

Gov. Manning will attend the conference of governors to be held in Boston August 24-27.

The total sales of liquor in the 15 dispensary counties for the month of July were $245,516.99.

The federal government has allotted $48,766.05 to the South Carolina militia for the year 1916.

Lewis W. Parker, of Greenville, has become assistant editor of the Greenville Evening Piedmont.

The governor has appointed special judges to hold all the courts assigned to Judge Spain for a year to come.

Victor, the 6-year-old child of Harry C. McLendon, was drowned in a reservoir at the Granby mills, Columbia, on Saturday.

Labin Mauldin, of Easley, who died last week, left the bulk of his estate, amounting to $13,000, to the Connie Maxwell Orphanage at Greenwood.

J. B. Halfacre has been named by Governor Manning as auditor of Newberry county, vice E. S. Wertz, who was suspended from office for alleged misconduct.
L. C. Harris, inspector on the Atlantic Coast Line road, fell under a switch engine at Florence Saturday while trying to get on it while in motion, and his leg was so crushed that it had to be amputated.

A row occurred in a Greenville negro house on Friday night over the suitableness of the coffin provided for a dead man; the police were called in to quell the disturbance, and found 17 pints of whiskey in the house.

After causing a good deal of trouble throughout the day, Fat Ward, a negro, was finally arrested in Spartanburg county Monday, and had to be spirited away to jail to prevent summary vengeance being wrought on him.

Joe Malloy, a negro convicted in Marlboro of the murder of two white boys, Guy Rogers and Prestiss Moore, in 1910, has been granted a respite from electrocution from August 18 to September 29. Affidavits were furnished the governor alieging that other parties had been heard to admit the killing. The respite is for the purpose of investigating these affidavits.
fat-ward-greer-1915-08.A3:
NEGRO ESCAPES MOB.
Finds Safety in Jail at Spartanburg.
Spartanburg, Aug. 16.—Fat Ward, a negro who bears the reputation of being a desperate character, was brought to the Spartanburg jail early this morning, having been spirited away from Greer to escape a mob which gathered outside the lockup Sunday night, bent, it is said, on taking vengeance for an attack on the town officers made about 9 o'clock when they were attempting to arrest him. According to report the negro had been causing more or less trouble throughout the day. When the officers surrounded him, it is said that he fired five shots, none of which took effect. A bullet passed through his shoulder at the same time. The crowd collected after it was learned that the negro was being attended by Dr. W. T. Brockman, who, with the assistance of Officer Charles Littlefield, sped toward Spartanburg with the negro in an automobile before the crowd knew of their intention. Ward is alleged to have a criminal court record in Greenville county.

oklahoma-city-oklahoma-city-1915-08.A1:
WHITE LABOR WILL BE USED AT CAPITOL BUILDING
Oklahoma City, Aug. 4.—What promised to be a serious labor difficulty at the very start of the new construction company's work on the capitol building was averted Wednesday when a committee from the local trades council met with Stewart company Superintendent Rice on the capitol grounds.

As a result of this conference it was agreed that white labor should be employed in the unskilled division of the construction work, and that this labor should belong to the Hod Carriers', Building and Common Laborers' union of North America, an organization affiliated with the American Federation of Labor. It is this organization that has done practically all the work on the capitol up to date. Construction under direction of the Stewart company started Wednesday, that company's contract having been signed yesterday afternoon.
